title: ParoQuant: Rotate Weights to Compress Reasoning Models for Fast Answers
one_liner: Reasoning models stay accurate at low precision by rotating weight groups so all numbers have similar sizes before compression.
lead: Large reasoning models are huge and slow. To run them quickly, you compress weights (which are the numbers the model has learned) by storing them with fewer bits of information. The problem: some weights are 1000 times bigger than others, so when you force them all into the same number of bins, tiny weights disappear and huge ones still take up half the space. Errors add up across a chain of 100 reasoning steps. ParoQuant solves this by rotating pairs of weights (a mathematical tweak that keeps the model's answers the same but spreads the weight sizes evenly), then compressing. With tricks to make the rotation fast on graphics chips and smart code, it stays nearly as quick as simpler methods while keeping answers right.

problem.h2: Squeezing weights breaks when sizes are wild
paras: Reasoning models have weights (learned numbers) that vary crazily in size. A beginner would compress all of them the same way: divide the range from smallest to biggest into equal steps. But if some weights are 1000 times bigger, tiny weights disappear and big ones still waste space. Each step of reasoning reads from the previous step, so a small error in step 1 becomes biased input to step 2, which adds its own error. After 100 steps, errors explode.
The compression is called quantization. Naive quantization treats all weights equally, which ruins accuracy on long reasoning chains.

steps.text: Scan weight groups where sizes vary wildly from tiny to huge.
Apply paired rotations to balance sizes. Model computes the same answer.
Divide by the max size in each group so all sizes land in one narrow range.
Weights now fit well in low-bit storage. No bits wasted on outliers.
Merge rotation and compression into one graphics chip routine. No overhead.

paras: The paper rotates pairs of weights before compression. Each rotation is a mathematical tweak that spins two weights without changing the model's final answer. These rotations flatten the wild size differences so all weights end up in the same ballpark.

hidden.name: size spread (biggest weight divided by smallest)
paras: Size spread is how much bigger the largest weight is than the smallest. If it is 1000 to 1, compression wastes bins on huge outliers and squashes tiny weights to zero. ParoQuant measures this in each group (weights that feed one output) and shrinks it.
The paper finds the biggest and smallest weight in each group, then designs rotations to make them closer together before compression.

heat.caption: Darker means bigger weight. Before rotation w1 is 16 times heavier than w2. After rotation, all close.

reads.html: Weights are like a bar graph. Tall bars waste compression bins. Rotation makes all bars the same height.
Size spread is the ratio of biggest to smallest in each weight group. Paired rotations shrink this ratio.

mechanism.h2: Why flattening stops errors from piling up
paras: Compression divides a range into bins. If weights span 0 to 100 using 16 bins, each bin is width 6.25. A weight at 95 lands in bin 15 with small error. But a weight at 1 falls between bins 0 and 1 and vanishes. Rotation spreads weights so they all land in the usable middle bins, where each bin measures a small difference.

In reasoning models, each layer reads output from the previous layer. A tiny compression error in layer 1 becomes wrong input to layer 2, which adds more error, spiraling. By evening out weight sizes first, ParoQuant keeps each layer's error tiny, so they don't pile up across 100 reasoning steps.

math.words: compressed_weight equals rounded value of rotated_weight divided by scale
math.equation: w_c = round(R(w) / s) where R is paired rotation, s is group scale
symbols: scale factor for the weight group
round to nearest integer for compression

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Group has 4 weights: 0.5, 2, 3, 80. Size spread is 80 divided by 0.5 = 160 to 1.
After rotation and scaling: 25, 26, 27, 28. Size spread now is 28 divided by 25 = 1.12 to 1.
Compress to 4-bit: 25, 26, 27, 28 round to bins 25, 26, 27, 28. Perfect.
Naive: compress 0.5, 2, 3, 80 with 16 bins. 0.5 goes to bin 0 and vanishes. 80 hits bin 15. Error huge.

math.note: Rotation keeps the model's math the same but reorganizes weights so compression spreads their bits fairly.

charts.title: Naive compression
charts.note: Errors in step 1 corrupt step 2, which corrupts step 3. Failure on long chains.

charts.title: With ParoQuant
charts.note: Even weight sizes keep errors small. Errors do not pile up across steps.

items.html: If the graphics chip code doesn't merge rotation and decompression into one operation, rotation overhead cancels the speed gain. ParoQuant builds them together into one routine.

items.b: Scaling per group loses ties between groups.
items.html: If weight groups are linked (one group's size depends on another), scaling each alone may hurt. Rare in practice on wide models.

items.b: New outliers appear if you retrain.
items.html: If you adjust the compressed model more, new huge weights can grow, erasing the rotation benefit. Re-rotate before retraining.

items.b: Done right: rotation and fused code.
items.html: Keeps running speed fast, keeps answers accurate, and works even after retraining when you rotate again.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a reasoning model like Llama or Qwen. Compress one copy with naive uniform bins, another with ParoQuant. Run a test of reasoning tasks (math, puzzles, code) that need 10 or more steps to solve. Count how many times each model gets the right answer.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy equals right answers divided by total questions, times 100
demo.closing: The demo must show ParoQuant keeps accuracy high while naive compression fails, proving that even weight sizes stop errors from piling up.
